name: Bhupendra Thapa
reflection:
This week, I learned how to connect a frontend web application to a backend using Flask. I set up a Flask project on PythonAnywhere and created API routes that enable my Learning Journal PWA to store, load, edit, and delete reflections. I discovered how JSON data can be saved on the server and how the backend updates the file whenever new reflections are added or modified.

Additionally, I practiced using the JavaScript Fetch API to interact with the Flask backend. This experience helped me understand the functionality of HTTP methods such as GET, POST, PUT, and DELETE in a practical context. One of the key lessons I learned was how to debug errors during deployment on PythonAnywhere—such as resolving issues related to outdated JSON files, missing IDs, and routes not being refreshed until the web app is reloaded.
Ultimately, I enhanced my PWA by incorporating new features like delete, edit, and search, which deepened my understanding of how frontend and backend logic must collaborate. In summary, I gained confidence in developing a dynamic web application that interacts with a live backend server.

name: Bhupendra Thapa
reflection:
1. Why is the frontend–backend connection important?
The connection between the frontend and backend is crucial as it facilitates the transfer of data between the user interface and the server. The frontend is responsible for what the user sees and interacts with, while the backend handles the processing, storage, and management of data. Without this link, the application would be unable to save user inputs, retrieve past reflections, or update information in real-time. This connection allows the PWA to operate like a true application rather than merely a static webpage.

2. Which HTTP methods did you use in Flask, and why?
I used four HTTP methods in Flask:

GET – to load and display all reflections stored in the JSON file.

POST – to add a new reflection submitted through the form.

PUT – to update or edit an existing reflection when the user changes the name or text.

DELETE – to remove a reflection from the JSON storage.

These methods allowed the app to perform full CRUD operations (Create, Read, Update, Delete), making it more interactive and functional.

3. What is the difference between using Flask to store and load JSON data and reading JSON
directly in the browser?
When JSON is read directly in the browser, the data is stored locally, which does not allow for permanent saving or sharing. As a result, each user’s data remains isolated, and any stored information is lost when the browser cache is cleared.

In contrast, using Flask allows the JSON file to be hosted on the server, ensuring that the data is persistent and can be accessed by all users. The backend manages how data is created, loaded, modified, or deleted, offering enhanced security, organization, and reliability. Furthermore, Flask enables dynamic updates to the JSON file through API routes, a feature not available when accessing JSON directly in the browser.

4. Did you face any difficulties when running your project on PythonAnywhere? How did you
handle them?
Yes, I faced several difficulties:

The DELETE and GET routes were failing because an old reflections.json file did not include the new "id" fields.

PythonAnywhere continued using the old version of my code until I clicked Reload in the Web tab.

A corrupted or empty JSON file caused errors when Flask tried to load data.

I solved these issues by deleting the reflections.json file, reloading the Flask app, and allowing PythonAnywhere to recreate the file automatically. Checking the error logs also helped me identify problems and fix them quickly.


5. What extra feature did you build into your PWA with Flask, and why did you add it?
The extra feature I added was the ability to delete, edit, and search reflections. I added these features to make the web app more functional and user-friendly. Deleting allows users to remove mistakes, editing lets them update their entries, and searching helps them quickly find specific reflections. These features also helped me practice using PUT and DELETE methods in Flask and understand how full backend integration works.
